newsitem.title: USA: Clinton upbeat in California swing. [CORRECTED 23:13 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Clinton upbeat in California swing. [CORRECTED 23:13 GMT]

text.p: President Bill Clinton, upbeat after his debate with Republican rival Bob Dole, Thursday (Corrects day) sought to shore up his support in California -- a state where his wide lead has shown signs of narrowing lately.

Addressing an enthusiastic crowd of several thousand outside the county court house, Clinton said he enjoyed the 90-minute televised exchange with Dole because it let him talk about the future let Americans "go beyond the tired rhetoric of yesterday's politics."

Clinton and Dole squared off for their final debate before the Nov. 5 election on Wednesday night at the University of San Diego, with initial opinion polls suggesting the Republican's more aggressive attacks on the incumbent did little to win over voters.
A USA Today/CNN/Gallup poll found that 59 percent of Americans felt Clinton won the last debate of the campaign season, while 29 percent said Dole was the winner.
An ABC News survey had similar results, with 56 percent of respondents feeling Clinton had come out on top, while 27 percent said the Republican challenger had carried the day.

The president and his aides clearly were bouyed by the debate as Clinton's White House campaign focused on southern California, a state where he has seen a wide lead narrow in recent weeks, according to various surveys.

A statewide poll published Wednesday by the San Francisco Examiner found that 49 percent of likely California voters back Clinton while 37 percent supported Dole. Reform Party candidate Ross Perot and the Green Party's Ralph Nader each had 3 percent. Eight percent were undecided.
Clinton's lead of 12 points was down four points from a similar poll in September.

"The big question in 19 days is, whose going to show up," Clinton said in urging his supporters to cast ballots on Election Day. He added: "I talk a lot about our responsibility, it is your responsibility to go vote, your responsibility as a citizen, your responsibility to be there."
Clinton began his day with a jog along a San Diego beach that served as a reminder of the passions of those who oppose him. A red-headed woman followed after him repeatedly shouting insults.
"You're a disgrace to the office of the presidency, to your gender and to this nation," shouted Valerie Parker, 32, of Bloomington, Ind. "You're a draft-dodging, yellow-bellied liar."
Clinton, who initially did not hear her, first responded with a thumbs-up gesture, but then smiled awkwardly as her attitude became clear.

In what amounted to a symbolic gesture to show his determination to win the state, Clinton visited Orange County, a highly conservative area of California where voters traditionally have favoured the Republican politics of Ronald Reagan over anything Democrats have offered.
Later he was to appear in Los Angeles, which offers far more fertile ground for his efforts to reap votes. He also planned to attend fundraisers to help congressional candidates.
Clinton was to return early Friday to Washington, where he and campaign officials will reassess the situation heading into the final weeks of the re-election fight and decide their priorities.

Aides say Clinton has already made clear that he intends to campaign in states that traditionally have been conceded to Republicans in the past, like Florida and Texas -- in part because he hopes to assist Democrats running in congressional races.
